## Overview

The Guatemalan potato tuber moth, *Tecia solanivora*, reached Ecuador in
1996 and spread through the Andes. Its larvae feed in potato tubers, and
farmers move it over long distances in the sacks of seed potatoes they buy
and carry between villages. @Rebaudo2011 coupled a cellular automaton of the
moth in the Simiatug valley to farmer agents, and asked how farmers' travel
and their knowledge of pest control speed its invasion. They used the model
in workshops with the farmers themselves.

This implementation is a **reproduction** of the model the authors published
as NetLogo code, with its landscape. That code is a simplified version of the
model their article describes, and the two differ in several rules, listed at
the end. One detail matters for the comparisons below: the article measures
invasion speed as the generations until 5% of the cells are infested, but
does not say what makes a cell infested.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The valley

The landscape is 80 × 80 cells of 500 m, with 37 village cells. Simiatug,
where the moths start, is the largest (the code gives it 3000 people and every
other village 500, figures its authors call invented):

```{julia}
land = potato_moth_landscape()
villages = findall(>(0), land.population)
p1 = heatmap(permutedims(land.temperature); c=:thermal, aspect_ratio=1,
             title="mean temperature (°C)", titlefontsize=10, xticks=false, yticks=false)
scatter!(p1, [I[1] for I in villages], [I[2] for I in villages]; color=:white, ms=3,
         label="villages")
scatter!(p1, [50], [41]; color=:cyan, marker=:star5, ms=7, label="Simiatug")
p2 = plot(-2:0.1:26, t -> potato_moth_survival(t, defaults(build(:potato_moth_farmers)));
          xlabel="temperature (°C)", ylabel="survival of a generation", label="",
          lw=2, title="survival against temperature", titlefontsize=10)
plot(p1, p2; layout=(1, 2), size=(800, 340), left_margin=3Plots.mm, bottom_margin=3Plots.mm)
```

Moths survive a generation only above about 13 °C, so the cold heights of the
valley, and Simiatug itself at 12 °C, hold almost none.

## The moths alone

Each generation, a share of the immatures dies, half of the survivors are
gravid females, farmers kill 10% of these, 30% of them fly to the four
neighbouring cells, and those in a cell lay the next generation's immatures,
up to a ceiling of 1000. Without farmers the moths spread only by flight:

```{julia}
alone = solve(problem(:potato_moth_farmers; farmers=0, generations=40); saveat=10)
heatmap(hcat([permutedims(log10.(u.immature .+ 1e-12)) for u in alone.u[2:end]]...);
        c=:viridis, clims=(-12, 3), xticks=false, yticks=false, size=(860, 250),
        title="log10 immatures at generations 10, 20, 30 and 40", titlefontsize=10)
```

The moths spread a cell a generation, and build up only where it is warm.
Every cell they reach keeps some moths, however few, so what counts as
infested decides how soon 5% of the valley is:

```{julia}
baseline = problem(:potato_moth_farmers; farmers=0)
[(threshold=h, generations=potato_moth_invasion_time(baseline; threshold=h))
 for h in (0, 1e-6, 0.01, 1, 10)]
```

Counting any moths, as the code's stopping rule does, takes 13 generations;
counting a cell from one immature, 19. The article's baseline is about 16.

## Farmers carrying moths

Each generation the farmers make several journeys between villages. A
farmer at a cell with moths buys infested seed potatoes unless its pest
control knowledge protects it; a farmer carrying moths leaves 90 immatures in
any cell without them. In the code every farmer buys infested potatoes. Half
the farmers are a red team, half a blue one, and a cell keeps the colour of
whoever first brought it moths:

```{julia}
prob = problem(:potato_moth_farmers; farmers=10, moves=4, seed=2, generations=12)
run = solve(prob; saveat=4)
colours = cgrad([:white, :green, :red, :blue], 4; categorical=true)
plot([heatmap(permutedims(u.source .* (u.immature .> 1)); c=colours, clims=(0, 3),
              aspect_ratio=1, colorbar=false, xticks=false, yticks=false,
              title="generation $(Int(t))", titlefontsize=10)
      for (t, u) in zip(run.t[2:end], run.u[2:end])]...; layout=(1, 3), size=(820, 290))
```

Cells with more than one immature, coloured by where their moths came from:
flight from the first infestation (green) or a farmer of either team. Farmers
plant new foci across the warm part of the valley, which then grow and merge.

```{julia}
potato_moth_counts.(run.u)
```

## Journeys and farmers

The article's Fig. 3 gives the generations to 5% infested for 1 to 10 journeys
a generation and 2 to 20 farmers. Ten runs each, counting a cell infested from
one immature:

```{julia}
speed(; runs=10, threshold=1, kwargs...) =
    mean(fetch.([Threads.@spawn potato_moth_invasion_time(
                     problem(:potato_moth_farmers; seed=s, kwargs...); threshold)
                 for s in 1:runs]))
moves = 1:10
crowds = (2, 10, 20)
grid = [speed(; farmers=n, moves=m) for m in moves, n in crowds]
plot(moves, grid; marker=:circle, lw=2, label=permutedims(["$n farmers" for n in crowds]),
     xlabel="journeys a generation", ylabel="generations to 5% infested",
     ylims=(0, 20), size=(650, 380))
hline!([19]; color=:gray, ls=:dash, label="no farmers")
scatter!([1, 2, 3, 4, 10], [15.9, 14.4, 13.7, 11.6, 8.8]; color=1, marker=:x, ms=6,
         label="source, 2 farmers")
scatter!([1, 2, 3, 4, 10], [12.0, 9.3, 7.0, 6.7, 5.3]; color=3, marker=:x, ms=6,
         label="source, 20 farmers")
```

The crosses are read from the article's Fig. 3. As there, farmers speed the
invasion most over the first few journeys, after which more journeys change
little, and more farmers speed it further. With 20 farmers the times agree
with the article's at every number of journeys, and with 2 farmers at 10
journeys. With 2 farmers making fewer journeys they are half a generation to
two generations longer, as the spread by flight alone is three (19
generations against the article's 16): the article's moths spread faster on
their own.

With 10 farmers making 4 journeys, the article's intermediate case, the
invasion is more than twice as fast as by flight alone, as the article finds:

```{julia}
(farmers_10_moves_4=grid[4, 2], no_farmers=19)
```

## Where carriers go

The code sends a farmer at a cell with moths to the village that minimises
its population times its distance: in effect the nearest small village. The
article's Fig. 4 counts the villages visited by farmers carrying moths, and
finds nearly all visits at Simiatug and the village nearest it (about 0.46 and
0.41). Here, over 20 generations of ten runs with 10 farmers making 4
journeys, counting where carriers stand at the end of each generation:

```{julia}
function stops(; runs=10, generations=20)
    visits = zeros(Int, 80, 80)
    for s in 1:runs
        integ = init(problem(:potato_moth_farmers; farmers=10, moves=4, seed=s,
                             generations); save_everystep=false)
        for _ in 1:generations
            step!(integ)
            for I in eachindex(integ.u.carriers)
                visits[I] += count_ones(integ.u.carriers[I])
            end
        end
    end
    return visits
end
visits = stops()
shares = sort([(village=land.village[I], cell=Tuple(I),
                share=round(visits[I] / sum(visits); digits=3)) for I in villages];
              by=x -> -x.share)
(simiatug=only(filter(x -> x.cell == (50, 41), shares)).share, most_visited=first(shares, 4))
```

This does not reproduce the article's figure. The visits spread over many
villages, none taking more than about 6%; Simiatug, in the cold where moths
barely survive, takes little. As the moths spread, carriers stand in cells
with moths throughout the warm part of the valley, and the nearest-village rule
sends them back and forth between neighbouring villages everywhere. The
article does not give the settings of its Fig. 4, and may have counted its
visits early in a run, before the moths had spread.

## Pest control knowledge

The article's Fig. 5 varies the farmers' pest control knowledge: its mean from
0 to 100 and its spread (standard deviation) from 0 to 30, with 2, 4 or 6
journeys. The code has no such option: every farmer buys infested potatoes.
Here knowledge is drawn from a normal distribution, kept within 0 and 100, and
a farmer buys infested potatoes with probability `1 - knowledge/100`. The
article gives no rule, and does not say how many farmers it used; we use 10.

```{julia}
means = 0:20:100
spreads = (0, 10, 30)
fig5 = Dict(m => [speed(; farmers=10, moves=m, knowledge=(μ, σ), infection=:probability)
                  for μ in means, σ in spreads]
            for m in (2, 4, 6))
plot([plot(means, fig5[m]; marker=:circle, lw=1.5, ylims=(0, 20),
           label=permutedims(["sd $σ" for σ in spreads]), legend=m == 2 ? :topleft : false,
           xlabel="mean knowledge", ylabel=m == 2 ? "generations to 5%" : "",
           title="$m journeys", titlefontsize=10) for m in (2, 4, 6)]...;
     layout=(1, 3), size=(850, 320), left_margin=4Plots.mm, bottom_margin=5Plots.mm)
```

```{julia}
[(journeys=m, knowledge_0=round(fig5[m][1, 1]; digits=1),
  knowledge_100_sd_10=round(fig5[m][end, 2]; digits=1),
  knowledge_100_sd_30=round(fig5[m][end, 3]; digits=1),
  knowledge_100_sd_0=fig5[m][end, 1]) for m in (2, 4, 6)]
```

The article finds about 10 to 12, 7.4 to 8.4 and 6.4 to 7 generations with no
knowledge for 2, 4 and 6 journeys, rising with knowledge to about 13.5 to
15.4, 11.8 to 13.8 and 9.7 to 12.2 at a mean of 100 with some spread. The runs
here agree, except with 2 journeys and a small spread of knowledge (17
generations against at most 15.4). As in the article, low knowledge nearly doubles the speed of
invasion, the spread of knowledge matters little except at high knowledge,
and a single farmer of low knowledge among knowledgeable ones speeds the
invasion considerably: with every farmer's knowledge at 100 nobody carries
moths, and the invasion is that of flight alone (19 generations here, 16 in
the article).
